name: Wei Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What's a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wei Evans, 43, and I'm a junior on a crew doing timber framing and general site jobs. I left school early and came into this trade later, so I still ask the lead to check my angles and cuts. I lay out fixings, carry timber and help close walls; I like seeing a room take its proper shape. The worst bit is a mistake discovered after the boards are up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are work and home connected for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner June works at a parcel counter, and our children are five and fourteen. We pay a mortgage and have roughly three and a half months of expenses saved. My wage is normal for a site hand and there are some other firms nearby, but a new job would take time. I use AI every day to turn marked-up drawings into a cut-list draft, then compare it with the lead's measurements before anything is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the phone earns its place when it catches a missing piece before we climb the stairs. It doesn't cut a straight stud for me, and I still check the chalk marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the site job and my wage to carry on. Even so, the parcel counter can have short hours and our three-and-a-half-month reserve is not endless, so I would not treat a quiet building season as harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking my present shifts and use AI to draft cut lists on straightforward rooms. In the first year I'd save the corrected lists beside my paper notes, so I can see whether the tool actually reduces second trips for timber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about ordinary income gaps, not the AI itself. A faster list makes my day easier, but it doesn't make the mortgage smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake did the phone catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a nursery room last month it flagged that I had five studs for six marked spaces. The lead confirmed the extra length before we sent the runner to the supplier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep paper notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to know which correction came from a real measurement. If the phone changes its answer next week, the notebook still tells me what we built.

say: I would tell coworkers that AI can catch **missing pieces** before a climb.
I would still check **chalk marks** before cutting timber.
think: My **site wage** should continue in a mild AI world.
Short parcel-counter hours and a **limited reserve** leave a quiet season worrying.
do: Keep **present paid shifts** on framing sites.
Compare **AI cut lists** with corrected paper notes on simple rooms.
feel: **Uneasy** about ordinary income gaps, while finding the tool useful.
S0.quote: A faster list makes my day easier, but it doesn't make the mortgage smaller.
fieldNote: Wei uses **AI daily** in a narrow, measurable way and preserves paper notes to identify real corrections.
He expects **site wages** to continue, but variable household hours keep the mortgage in view even under a plateau.

steps.text: Keep taking paid framing shifts on current sites
Save corrected AI cut lists beside paper measurements for simple rooms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager to let one crew test a new schedule and publish the actual hours before calling it a saving. If the office can order faster, we should know whether that means fewer hands on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might become useful checking AI lists against the site, but I am still a junior worker who can be sent home first. If a contractor squeezes crew hours, my wage could dip while June's parcel-counter income is also uneven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to run the new schedule on one small framing job and record planned hours against actual hours. In the first year I'd keep site shifts, ask the lead for paid practice on accurate setting-out, and apply to another builder if our weekly rota falls below four days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like testing a tool, but a successful trial is no comfort if the reward is one less paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count as success?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The timber arrives before we need it and the job uses fewer wasted hours without cutting a worker's pay. I would put both figures in the same notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why setting-out practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lead can spot a bowed corner before I do. If I can set out a whole room accurately, I have something more to offer than carrying boards.

say: I would ask for a **site trial** and actual hours before claiming savings.
I would ask whether faster buying means **smaller crews**.
think: My **junior hours** could fall even if I help check AI lists.
June’s variable **counter income** would make a wage dip harder.
do: Test a **new schedule** on one framing job and record hours.
Seek **paid setting-out practice** with the lead.
Apply to **another builder** if weekly shifts drop below four.
feel: **Anxious** that efficiency could reduce my paid rota.
S1.quote: I like testing a tool, but a successful trial is no comfort if the reward is one less paid shift.
fieldNote: He welcomes **controlled trials** but measures worker hours as well as delivery speed.
His **junior status** and June’s variable pay make a smaller rota a direct household risk.

steps.text: Test AI schedule on one framing job and record planned versus actual hours
Ask lead for paid setting-out practice
Apply to another builder if weekly rota drops below four days
Keep current paid site shifts during the trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell June that AGI in 2028 can handle the cut lists and drawings, and robots that can fit timber come around 2031. My phone skill is not a second trade when all the phones get that clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning bits of my day could disappear first, though I should still earn lifting and fitting until robots reach the site. By 2031 I expect my junior shifts to be cut sharply, and our reserve won't cover years of mortgage and children's costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask an energy-retrofit contractor about paid trainee work sealing and insulating older homes, and apply if there is a wage. In 2029 I'd keep framing shifts, use AGI lists only after measuring the room, and ask June to review the mortgage terms with me; if site hours actually drop, we'd contact the lender before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can move early, but there's a real chance the wage I move toward gets automated too before the mortgage is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is retrofit work safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a few years because older walls are awkward, but capable robots could seal and insulate as well. I want a paid test of the market, not a certificate sold as shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we may have to skip the holiday this year while I try a paid route into another job. I won't ask the fourteen-year-old to carry our mortgage worry.

say: I would explain that **2028 AGI** takes lists before **2031 robots** fit timber.
I would tell June that my **phone skill** alone cannot secure wages.
think: My **planning tasks** could disappear before hands-on work.
I expect my **junior shifts** to shrink sharply once robots arrive.
do: Apply for **paid retrofit training** if a contractor offers wages.
Keep **framing shifts** and check AGI lists against rooms in 2029.
Review **mortgage terms** with June and contact the lender if hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** because both current and replacement wages may be threatened.
S2.quote: My phone skill is not a second trade when all the phones get that clever.
fieldNote: He understands **2028 thinking AI** removes his digital edge before physical robots threaten his main wages.
His retrofit idea is a **paid experiment**, and he explicitly doubts that awkward buildings guarantee lasting safety.

steps.text: Apply for paid energy-retrofit trainee work if wages are offered
Check AGI lists against room measurements in 2029
Contact mortgage lender with June if site hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us run real paid trials instead of buying a miracle course. AGI changes layouts in 2031, then robots can do the fitting around 2034; the gap matters if we use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I might still have site shifts after AGI takes the list-making, but the builder may expect a smaller crew. At 51, robots able to fit timber could remove the basic jobs I do; I expect my pay to fall unless I can show another employer useful work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take one paid Saturday a month with a local retrofit crew if they will supervise me, and keep my main framing shifts. By 2032 I'd record whether those jobs cover my travel and time and apply for a regular retrofit post; in the first year after 2031 I'd use AGI to check insulation orders while measuring every wall myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though the five years make a test possible. If the Saturday work only looks profitable before travel and supplies, I would rather know early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the retrofit supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether they can show me how to seal around an old window without trapping moisture. I would not take a client's money for that until someone had checked my first jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for one Saturday job a month. I would borrow tools on the supervised shifts and wait until a regular wage offer is real.

say: I would prefer **paid trials** over an untested course.
I would explain the gap between **2031 layouts** and **2034 fitting**.
think: My **crew hours** may narrow after AGI changes planning.
My **basic fitting pay** could fall heavily when robots reach sites.
do: Work **paid supervised retrofit Saturdays** while keeping framing shifts.
Apply for a **regular retrofit post** by 2032 if the work pays.
Use **AGI insulation orders** with physical measurements after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test the true earnings of another trade.
S3.quote: If the Saturday work only looks profitable before travel and supplies, I would rather know early.
fieldNote: Wei tests **real earnings** after travel and supplies, resisting a van purchase before there is steady paid demand.
He places **AGI planning** ahead of 2034 robots and recognises that basic fitting is his main income exposure.

steps.text: Take one paid supervised retrofit Saturday monthly if offered
Apply for regular retrofit post by 2032 if earnings justify it
Use AGI insulation orders with wall measurements after 2031
Keep main paid framing shifts during the trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children they'll be older before the robots reach our tools, but their parents will still need to earn. I'll be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036 and 56 when fitting robots arrive around 2039, which is not a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be fifteen and twenty-four by 2036, so the older one may have left home while the younger still needs school support. The mortgage may be smaller, but I expect site wages to narrow after 2039; I don't know of a pension that would make that harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building work now, add part of every full-pay month to savings, and test paid retrofit jobs without buying a van. In 2037 I'd compare a real retrofit wage offer with my site pay and use AGI for ordering only if the measurements check out; if the new work has enough customers, I'd apply before robots reach fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy today. A decade is time to build proof, but I'd be a fool to spend it assuming someone will always pay for a junior pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with a small fixed share of each full-pay month, not money we need for the mortgage or groceries. If June's counter hours fall, I would pause the extra saving rather than claim the same amount is still possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your older child contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if they choose to, but I would not budget for it. At twenty-four they may be paying for their own home or training.

say: I would tell the children that **age 56** still calls for work.
I would seek **real retrofit wages** before robots reach fitting.
think: The children’s **school costs** change as they grow older.
My **site income** may narrow after 2039 without a guaranteed pension.
do: Keep **paid building work** and save from full-pay months.
Test **paid retrofit jobs** without buying a van.
Use checked **AGI orders** and compare wage offers in 2037.
feel: **Uneasy** about later income, with years to gather proof.
S4.quote: A decade is time to build proof, but I'd be a fool to spend it assuming someone will always pay for a junior pair of hands.
fieldNote: He ages his children correctly and does not use **adult-child income** or a pension as a hidden safety net.
His **adaptive approach** still requires paid demand and protects the mortgage before any equipment purchase.

steps.text: Keep earning paid framing wages on building sites
Save a small share of each full-pay month when bills allow
Test paid supervised retrofit jobs without buying a van
Apply for regular retrofit post after comparing 2037 wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because my cut-list trick stops being valuable almost at once and robots reach the fitting work by 2031. Paid trainee hours with a retrofit crew and clear notice from my contractor would help. I'd need to keep the framing wage while I learn; three and a half months of savings will not fund a whole career change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who has to correct an AI list when the order is wrong. On my site it's usually the junior worker carrying the replacement timber up the stairs. I'd like the person who approves the list to see that hour written down too.

headlineQuote: On my site it's usually the junior worker carrying the replacement timber up the stairs.
portrait: Wei is a **43-year-old junior** framer still developing his carpentry skills after leaving school early.
A **mortgage**, two school-age children and variable counter hours limit his three-and-a-half-month reserve.
He uses **AI daily**, comparing cut lists and schedules with measured site results.
He tests **paid retrofit work** while keeping framing wages and watching robot competition.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** quickly removes his cut-list edge and threatens his fitting wages when robots arrive by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retrofit trainee hours** and clear staffing notice would let him learn while retaining wages.
